description: An AI-powered Mars rover mission planning tool that balances scientific discovery, terrain safety, and safe return.
summary: MarsMind helps future Mars crews answer a practical question before leaving base: Can we reach a science target and still have enough oxygen, battery power, and time to return? Our interactive prototype uses NASA Mars Trek imagery and terrain slope derived from USGS elevation data to plan routes across Jezero Crater. Users compare routes by distance, terrain risk, and science opportunities. In a simulated battery shortage, MarsMind marks where the crew should turn back, showing how a change in available power can alter the mission plan.
details:
MarsMind is an interactive prototype for planning a Marswalk in Jezero Crater. Users choose a science destination and optional waypoints, then compare the shortest route, a lower-risk route, and an option that visits more science targets. For each plan, MarsMind estimates travel time, oxygen use, and battery use for the full round trip.

The map uses NASA Mars Trek imagery, including MRO CTX and HiRISE images of Jezero Crater. MarsMind derives terrain slope from the USGS Mars 2020 TRN CTX elevation model (DOI 10.5066/P906QQT8). It aggregates slope from the source model’s 20 m pixel spacing onto a 125 m planning grid. The A* planner avoids cells above a configurable slope threshold and weighs terrain risk when choosing a route.

MarsMind lets users see how a change in resources affects the decision to keep going or turn back. In the default simulation, the trip to Delta front and back covers 6.97 km and leaves 67% battery. When available battery capacity drops by 75%, the map marks where the crew would need to turn back to preserve its modeled return reserve. Future crews could use this approach to rehearse decisions before an excursion. Suit resources, slope limits, and science priorities are configurable assumptions.

We built the planner in Python with NumPy and used Streamlit and Plotly for the interactive interface. The release passed 90 automated tests, including checks against live NASA data endpoints. Claude Code and OpenAI Codex assisted with development and review, and Kokoro TTS generated the demo’s English narration.
